findings.summary: The unprefixed spelling require('assert') loads the same loose module and passes the guard
findings.recommendation: Scope: class - BARE_REQUIRE in scripts/assert-strict-guard.js matches exactly one spelling, `require(<quote>node:assert<quote>)` on one line, so it checks the spelling rather than the module. Members: (1) `require('assert')` with no `node:` prefix - the most common Node idiom and what a suite written from any non-repo template or example brings; (2) dynamic `import('node:assert')`; (3) a require whose argument sits on its own line. None occurs in test/ today (searched all 593 files), so nothing is currently hidden, but (1) is a one-token route to exactly the regrowth the issue exists to stop, and CONTRIBUTING.md now tells contributors the suite enforces `node:assert/strict`. The Architect's wording names `require('node:assert')` literally, so this is a gap against the issue's purpose, not its letter. Fix (1) by making the prefix optional (`(?:node:)?assert`) with a negative fixture alongside the existing ones, and have the remedy line still say node:assert/strict; (2) and (3) are exotic enough to accept on the record.

findings.summary: The comment exemption exempts some real requires
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance - inComment() decides from the line alone. A real require evades when (a) the line begins with a closed block comment (`/* x */ const assert = require('node:assert');`), (b) any `//` precedes it on the line, including inside a string (`const u = 'http://h', assert = require('node:assert');`), or (c) the line begins with `*` as a continued expression. All three need unusual code and none exists in test/; no test file at HEAD mentions the bare module in a comment either, so the exemption currently protects nothing and only fails open. Cheapest tightening if wanted: for the `/*` case, treat the hit as commented only when no `*/` precedes it on the line. Otherwise accept; the false-positive direction (prose inside an unstarred block comment line is flagged) fails closed.

findings.summary: Waiver handling differs from its description in three small ways
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. (1) CHANGELOG.md says a waiver 'is reported when the check runs'; that holds for `node scripts/assert-strict-guard.js`, but the in-suite test only passes guard.report() as the failure message, so on a green CI run a waiver prints nowhere - it is visible in source only. (3) docs/waivers.md also accepts an em dash separator; this checker takes only `--`, so an em-dash waiver is treated as an offender (fails closed). None changes what anyone does today since no waiver exists; if (1) matters, print the waived lines from the suite test via t.diagnostic.
